Get started with quarantineRisk

Source: vignettes/get-started.Rmd
get-started.Rmd

Who this is for: public health students and policy analysts. Question: for a variant with a given transmissibility (R₀), how much vaccine efficacy (VE) is needed to keep border-quarantine breach risk at or below an acceptable level, compared with the pre-Delta baseline?

Installation 

# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-yfan0161-stack")
library(quarantineRisk)
library(ggplot2)

The data

quarantine_risk holds model results adapted from Zachreson et al. (2022) for R₀ from 1 to 10 and VE from 0 to 0.9.

head(quarantine_risk)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>      R0    VE beta_ratio
#>   <int> <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1     1   0       0.163 
#> 2     1   0.1     0.143 
#> 3     1   0.2     0.132 
#> 4     1   0.3     0.127 
#> 5     1   0.4     0.0972
#> 6     1   0.5     0.0607
Field Meaning
R0 Basic reproduction number (average number of people one case infects)
VE Vaccine efficacy (0 = no protection, 0.9 = 90% reduction)
beta_ratio Total infection force relative to the pre-Delta unvaccinated baseline (1 = baseline)

beta_ratio is a relative multiplier, not a probability. In this dataset the baseline value of 1 is reached at R₀ = 3 with no vaccination.

Calculate risk for one scenario 

calculate_risk(r0 = 6, ve = 0.6)
#> [1] 0.74
calculate_risk(r0 = 6, ve = 0.5)
#> [1] 1.01
calculate_risk(r0 = 6, ve = 0.3)
#> [1] 1.82

Values below 1 are better than the baseline; values above 1 mean elevated breach risk. Values between grid points are linearly interpolated.

Find the vaccine efficacy needed 

find_threshold_ve(r0 = 6, target = 1)
#> [1] 0.504
find_threshold_ve(r0 = 6, target = 0.5)
#> [1] 0.654

At R₀ = 6, VE must reach about 0.504 to keep risk at or below the baseline. If the target cannot be met even at VE = 0.9, the function returns NA:

find_threshold_ve(r0 = 10, target = 0.1)
#> [1] NA
ve <- seq(0, 0.9, by = 0.01)
d <- data.frame(VE = ve, risk = calculate_risk(6, ve))
ggplot(d, aes(VE, risk)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2d6a4f", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = find_threshold_ve(6), linetype = "dotted", colour = "#c1121f") +
  labs(x = "Vaccine efficacy", y = "Risk (× baseline)",
       subtitle = "R0 = 6; dashed = baseline, dotted = minimum VE") +
  theme_minimal()

Launch the Shiny app 

run_app()

Controls

  • R₀ slider: transmissibility of the variant.
  • VE slider: vaccine efficacy in the population.
  • Acceptable risk: your tolerance as a multiple of the baseline (must be greater than 0; otherwise the app shows a message).

Outputs and how to read them

  • The risk card compares the modelled risk at your R₀ and VE with your target (green = below, amber = about equal, red = above).
  • The minimum VE card gives the lowest VE that reaches your target at that R₀. This directly answers the app’s question.
  • In the heatmap, dark green is low risk and yellow/red is high. The dashed line marks your target: combinations above and to the left of it (high VE, low R₀) meet the target; those below and to the right exceed it. The white dot is your selection.
  • The line plot is a slice of the heatmap at your R₀; the dotted line shows the minimum VE.

If you enter an acceptable risk that is empty, zero or negative, the app asks you to correct it. If the target cannot be met at any modelled VE, the app says so and suggests a higher tolerance or a lower R₀.

Limitations

  • Results are relative risks from published simulations of low-tolerance quarantine systems, not probabilities of a breach.
  • The data is a 10 × 10 grid with linear interpolation between points, and the simulation output contains some noise.
  • The package is for exploring scenarios, not for operational decisions.
